Yes, those hollow fiber blankets and bed rolls are good down to somewhat below freezing and fine inside a vehicle. Just remember, don't ever put your head under the covers. What will happen is first, you're breathing too much CO2. It lowers your brain function, can cause unhealthy types of sleep and reduces your alertness when you wake up but what's far worse is that the moisture from your breath will condense inside your bedding and you will lose much of the heat retention. You will end up cold, clammy and damp by the time you wake up in the morning. Basically, you'll be miserable and you'll need to dry out your bedding somehow which means you'll need heat. If you feel uncomfortable with cold on your face you can use a towel and leave your nose and mouth uncovered or if you have a bedroll with a draw string just tighten it up around your face. I know it's terrible tempting to duck your whole head in side your bedding but very bad in practice.

When you get a military bed roll look for the ones that come in three layers. The outer shell will be for water resistance when you have to use it without a tent or you can place it under the others to protect against ground moisture. Then you have a heavy one for subzero and a lighter one for down to around zero. When it's super cold you can use all three as they fit one inside the other.

Some of us don't like wearing regular clothes inside a bedroll and I'm one of those but putting your skin on the bed roll is a bad idea. It gives off moisture into your bedding and skin oils so it's great if you have long johns made of virgin wool. If you've never worn them in cold weather they are awesome. Very light and airy but retain heat in a wonderful way while letting your skin breathe. Cotton long johns are just not suitable. They absorb sweat and if they get wet you are ruined. Wool even if wet can be gently squeezed out and patted semi dry with towels and put back on while damp. Your body heat will easily dry them out. If you have two pairs even better. The wet ones can be carefully squeezed out and in sub zero temps simply hung up outside. The cold dry air will freeze dry them. When they thaw back out they will be mostly dry. Now you know why God gave sheep wool coats, right? The virgin wool comes from first cutting on lambs so it's very soft and not scratchy. Only one tip has the cut end while the other end is silky new. Coming from young lambs the fibers are more soft.

When you get a nice military bedroll you can put inside a good trash bag and store in your trunk if you have passengers.

If you turn into a skid and don't hit either the gas or the brakes you can roll out of a skid and regain control. Speaking of not putting your head inside your bedding, the last time I got really sick on a trip, I did exactly that! Temps dropped to 20º that night (we were in the desert) and I woke up with my nose ice cold with the back of my throat feeling numb. I had showered at the truck stop and rather than dry my hair after, I fell asleep with it wet in a towel. The towel slipped off in the middle of the night and my entire scalp was aching from the cold. I stuck my head inside my sleeping bag and tried to make a little airway for my mouth so that it wouldn't get so damp inside my sleeping bag. I slept fitfully alternating between letting cold air inside the sleeping bag or trying to breath the trapped humid air if I ducked my head in. I did manage to get in a short spurt of sleep but I had the start of a really bad sore throat when I woke up. You know how it starts as a little tickle or rawness in the back of your throat? And the deeper it is inside your throat, the worse you know it will be? I could tell this one was going to be a harsh cold and accelerate quickly and sure enough, it did. It didn't help that the day before, I had gotten a full body adjustment from a chiropractor who warned me I'd be sore a few days. All the conditions were less than optimal.
